'''''Ruellia simplex''''', the '''Mexican petunia''', '''Mexican bluebell''', '''Britton's wild petunia''', or '''Purple showers''',<ref>{{cite web |title=Ruellia simplex 'Purple Showers' |url=https://www.brookgreen.org/plant-collection/name/ruellia-simplex-purple-showers |website=Brookgreen Gardens |access-date=2026-06-06}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Acanthaceae]] that is native to [[Mexico]], the [[Caribbean]], and [[South America]]. It has become a widespread [[invasive species|invasive plant]] in [[Florida]], where it was likely introduced as an [[ornamental plant|ornamental]] before 1933,<ref name="FLIP">{{cite web|url=http://www.plantatlas.usf.edu/flip/plant.aspx?id=35|title=''Ruellia simplex''|work=FLIP (Florida Invasive Plants)|publisher=University of South Florida|access-date=5 September 2012|archive-date=23 April 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120423224746/http://www.plantatlas.usf.edu/flip/plant.aspx?id=35|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="ARS-GRIN">{{GRIN | accessdate = 14 January 2018}}</ref> as well as in the [[eastern Mediterranean]], [[South Asia]] and other parts of the [[Eastern Hemisphere]].

==Taxonomy and synonyms==
''Ruellia simplex'' ([[Charles_Wright_(botanist)|Wright]]) is the oldest and accepted name for this species, which has been variously called ''Ruellia angustifolia'' ([[Christian Gottfried Daniel Nees von Esenbeck|Nees]], [[Gustav Lindau |Lindau]]), ''Ruellia brittoniana'' ([[Emery Clarence Leonard|Leonard]]), and ''Cryphiacanthus angustifolius'' (Nees), among others.<ref name="PL">{{cite web|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl/record/kew-2420045|title=''Ruellia simplex'' C.Wright|work=The Kew Plant List|access-date=2012-09-05}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Manzitto-Tripp |first1=Erin A. |last2=Daniel |first2=Thomas F. |title=Phylogeny and revised classification of New World Ruellia |journal=Taxon |date=2023-07-23 |volume=72 |issue=5 |pages=1034–1056 |doi=10.1002/tax.13001 |bibcode=2023Taxon..72.1034M |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/tax.13001 |access-date=2026-06-06 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The genus is named after French botanist [[Jean Ruel]], while the specific name refers to the simple, not compound leaves.<ref name="PBS">{{cite web|url=http://www.plantbook.org/plantdata/acanthaceae/ruellia_simplex.html|title=''Ruellia simplex''|work=Landscape Plants for South Florida|publisher=Palm Beach State College|access-date=2012-09-05|archive-date=2014-08-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808052849/http://www.plantbook.org/plantdata/acanthaceae/ruellia_simplex.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Description==
''Ruellia simplex'' is an evergreen perennial growing {{convert|3|ft|m|abbr=on}} tall, forming colonies of stalks with lance-shaped leaves that are {{convert|6|to|12|in|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|.5|to|.75|in|cm|abbr=on}} wide. 

The flowers are metallic blue to purple, trumpet-shaped with an about {{convert|2|in|cm|abbr=on}}-wide, five-lobed [[petal|corolla]]. There is a dwarf variety that is only {{convert|1|ft|m|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name="FLIP" />

==Distribution==
''Ruellia simplex'' is native to Mexico, the West Indies, western Bolivia, southwestern Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, and northeastern Argentina. It has been widely used as an ornamental plant and has [[escaped plant|escaped from cultivation]] in the United States, Australia and parts of Asia, as well as several Pacific Islands.

It has become invasive in some of these areas, forming dense, single-species stands of vegetation which threaten native plants. It is mainly a plant of wet places such as ditches, pond verges, lakesides and marshes, but can survive in drier conditions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rojas-Sandoval |first1=Julissa |last2=Acevedo-Rodríguez |first2=Pedro |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/110307 |title=''Ruellia simplex'' (Mexican petunia) |date=2014 |journal=Invasive Species Compendium |volume=CABI Compendium |publisher=CABI |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.110307 |access-date=8 August 2020 |doi-access=free |archive-date=28 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028105202/https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/110307 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Control==
The University of Florida's [[Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences]] is trying to reduce the number of home gardeners who plant ''R. simplex'' by recommending alternatives, especially ''[[Silphium asteriscus]]'', ''[[Sisyrinchium angustifolium]]'', ''[[Stachytarpheta jamaicensis]]'', ''[[Stokesia laevis]]'', but also including some ''R. simplex'' cultivars that are sterile.<ref name="UFLA-IFAS-EDIS-garden-alts">{{cite web | title=ENH1207/EP468: Alternatives to Invasive Plants Commonly Found in Central Florida Landscapes | website=Electronic Data Information Source (EDIS) | publisher=[[Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences]] (IFAS), UF | date=2018-08-29 | url=http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/ep468 | access-date=2021-10-06 | archive-date=2021-10-06 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211006224341/https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/ep468 | url-status=live }}</ref>
